entry.title: Blog 18—The Push of Gravity: Deriving the CDM Euler Equation

link.title: Blog 18—The Push of Gravity: Deriving the CDM Euler Equation

entry.content:
Introduction

In our last exploration, we derived the continuity equation—the statement that mass is conserved as it flows through expanding spacetime. We watched how the density contrast \(\delta\) evolves due to the convergence of fluid flow and the stretching of conformal spacetime itself. But continuity alone cannot build structure; it tells us only that matter redistributes, not why it moves.

Today, we derive the Euler equation for Cold Dark Matter. If the continuity equation is the accounting of mass, the Euler equation is the physics of force. It tells us how gravitational potentials accelerate fluid elements, how the cosmic expansion dampens peculiar velocities, and how momentum conservation shapes the cosmic web.

We proceed from where we stood before. In Blog 17 we adopted conformal time \(\eta\) (with \(d\eta = dt/a\)), the Newtonian gauge with potentials \(\phi = \psi\), and defined the velocity divergence \( heta \equiv \partial_i v^i\) using the comoving peculiar velocity \(v^i = dx^i/d\eta\). We derived the continuity equation in that convention:

\[\delta' + heta - 3\phi' = 0\]

with primes denoting \(d/d\eta\). Today we turn to the spatial component of the conservation law, \( abla_\mu T^{\mu i} = 0\), and derive its dynamical partner.

Conventions Recap

Since notation is everything in perturbation theory, let us restate the essential conventions inherited from Blog 17:

  • Metric signature: \((-,+,+,+)\).
  • Time coordinate: conformal time \(\eta\), with \(d\eta = dt/a\). Primes denote \(\partial_\eta\).
  • Newtonian gauge metric:
\[ds^2 = a^2(\eta)\left[-(1+2\phi)d\eta^2 + (1-2\phi)\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j ight] ag{48}\]
  • Conformal Hubble parameter: \(\mathcal{H} \equiv a'/a = aH\).
  • Background density: satisfies \( ar{ ho}' + 3\mathcal{H} ar{ ho} = 0\), so \( ar{ ho} \propto a^{-3}\).
  • Comoving peculiar velocity: \(v^i \equiv dx^i/d\eta\) (a first-order perturbation).
  • Velocity divergence: \( heta \equiv \partial_i v^i\).

The Setup: Spatial Components of Conservation

The conservation of energy-momentum in General Relativity is expressed through the covariant divergence:

\[ abla_\mu T^{\mu i} = 0 ag{49}\]

In Blog 17 we examined the temporal component (\( u = 0\)) and obtained the continuity equation. Now we set \( u = i\), where \(i\) runs over the three spatial indices \((1, 2, 3)\). This gives us the evolution of momentum density—the Euler equation.

Expanding the covariant derivative:

\[ abla_\mu T^{\mu i} = \partial_\mu T^{\mu i} + \Gamma^\mu_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda i} + \Gamma^i_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda} = 0 ag{50}\]

For CDM (a pressureless perfect fluid),

\[T^{\mu u} = ho\, u^\mu u^ u ag{51}\]

where \( ho = ar{ ho}(1+\delta)\) is the total density and \(u^\mu\) is the 4-velocity.

The 4-Velocity in Conformal Newtonian Gauge

From the normalization condition \(u_\mu u^\mu = -1\) applied to the metric (48), the 4-velocity of a CDM element with comoving peculiar velocity \(v^i\) is, to first order,

\[u^\mu = rac{1}{a}\left(1 - \phi,\; v^i ight), \qquad u_\mu = a\left(-(1+\phi),\; v_i ight) ag{52}\]

The factor of \(1/a\) in \(u^\mu\) reflects the fact that \(\eta\) is a conformal time coordinate, and the perturbation \(-\phi\) in the time component is the gravitational time dilation. It is straightforward to verify \(u^\mu u_\mu = -1 + \mathcal{O}(2)\).

The Christoffel Symbols in Conformal Newtonian Gauge

From the metric (48), the non-zero Christoffel symbols to first order in \(\phi\) are:

\[\Gamma^0_{00} = \mathcal{H} + \phi', \qquad \Gamma^0_{0i} = \partial_i\phi, \qquad \Gamma^0_{ij} = \left[\mathcal{H}(1-2\phi) - \phi' ight]\delta_{ij} ag{53}\] \[\Gamma^i_{00} = \partial^i\phi, \qquad \Gamma^i_{0j} = \left(\mathcal{H} - \phi' ight)\delta^i_j, \qquad \Gamma^i_{jk} = -\delta^i_k\partial_j\phi - \delta^i_j\partial_k\phi + \delta_{jk}\partial^i\phi ag{54}\]

Of these, only \(\Gamma^0_{00}\), \(\Gamma^0_{0i}\), \(\Gamma^0_{ij}\), \(\Gamma^i_{00}\), and \(\Gamma^i_{0j}\) will contribute to the Euler equation at linear order. Note the appearance of \(\mathcal{H}\) inside \(\Gamma^0_{00}\) and \(\Gamma^i_{0j}\)—these are the conformal-time analogue of the \(H\) terms we saw in Blog 17, and they will combine into a Hubble drag below.

Evaluating the Terms

We now compute each piece of (50), keeping only linear terms in the perturbations.

The Partial Derivative Term \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu i}\)

This splits into time and space parts:

\[\partial_\mu T^{\mu i} = \partial_0 T^{0i} + \partial_j T^{ji} ag{55}\]

First, \(T^{0i} = ho u^0 u^i\). Using (52) and keeping only first-order terms:

\[T^{0i} = ho \cdot rac{1-\phi}{a}\cdot rac{v^i}{a} \approx rac{ ar{ ho}\, v^i}{a^2} ag{56}\]

where we drop the product \(\phi v^i\) (second order) and replace \( ho o ar{ ho}\) in a first-order term.

Now take the conformal-time derivative. Using \( ar{ ho}' = -3\mathcal{H} ar{ ho}\):

\[\partial_0 T^{0i} = \partial_\eta\!\left( rac{ ar{ ho}\,v^i}{a^2} ight) = rac{ ar{ ho}' v^i}{a^2} + rac{ ar{ ho}\,v'^i}{a^2} - rac{2a' ar{ ho}\,v^i}{a^3} = rac{ ar{ ho}}{a^2}\left(v'^i - 5\mathcal{H}v^i ight) ag{57}\]

Next, the spatial derivative term:

\[T^{ji} = ho\, u^j u^i = ho\, rac{v^j}{a} rac{v^i}{a} ag{58}\]

This is second order in \(v\), so we set:

\[\partial_j T^{ji} \approx 0 ag{59}\]

The Christoffel Contraction \(\Gamma^\mu_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda i}\)

This contracts the trace of the Christoffel symbols with the momentum density:

\[\Gamma^\mu_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda i} = \Gamma^\mu_{\mu 0}T^{0i} + \Gamma^\mu_{\mu j}T^{ji} ag{60}\]

The second term involves \(T^{ji}\), which is second order. For the first, we need the trace:

\[\Gamma^\mu_{\mu 0} = \Gamma^0_{00} + \Gamma^j_{j0} = \left(\mathcal{H}+\phi' ight) + 3\left(\mathcal{H}-\phi' ight) = 4\mathcal{H} - 2\phi' ag{61}\]

where we used (53) and (54) with \(j\) summed. Multiplying by \(T^{0i}\) (first order), the \(-2\phi'\) piece is second order and drops:

\[\Gamma^\mu_{\mu 0}T^{0i} \approx 4\mathcal{H}\cdot rac{ ar{ ho}\,v^i}{a^2} ag{62}\]

The Christoffel Curvature Term \(\Gamma^i_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda}\)

This is the term that will supply the gravitational force:

\[\Gamma^i_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda} = \Gamma^i_{00}T^{00} + \Gamma^i_{0j}T^{0j} + \Gamma^i_{j0}T^{j0} + \Gamma^i_{jk}T^{jk} ag{63}\]

The last term has \(\Gamma^i_{jk}\) (first order) contracted with \(T^{jk} \sim v^j v^k\) (second order), so it drops.

First piece: Using \(\Gamma^i_{00} = \partial^i\phi\) and \(T^{00} = ho (u^0)^2 \approx ar{ ho}/a^2\) (since \(\Gamma^i_{00}\) is already first order, we take the zeroth-order piece of \(T^{00}\)):

\[\Gamma^i_{00}T^{00} \approx rac{ ar{ ho}}{a^2}\,\partial^i\phi ag{64}\]

Second and third pieces: Using \(\Gamma^i_{0j} = (\mathcal{H}-\phi')\delta^i_j\):

\[\Gamma^i_{0j}T^{0j} = (\mathcal{H}-\phi') rac{ ar{ ho}\,v^i}{a^2} \approx rac{\mathcal{H} ar{ ho}\,v^i}{a^2} ag{65}\]

and by symmetry \(\Gamma^i_{j0} = \Gamma^i_{0j}\), so

\[\Gamma^i_{j0}T^{j0} \approx rac{\mathcal{H} ar{ ho}\,v^i}{a^2} ag{66}\]

Collecting:

\[\Gamma^i_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda} \approx rac{ ar{ ho}}{a^2}\left(\partial^i\phi + 2\mathcal{H}v^i ight) ag{67}\]

Assembling the Euler Equation

Substituting (57), (62), and (67) into (50) and multiplying through by \(a^2/ ar{ ho}\):

\[\left(v'^i - 5\mathcal{H}v^i ight) + 4\mathcal{H}v^i + \partial^i\phi + 2\mathcal{H}v^i = 0 ag{68}\]

The Hubble terms combine as \(-5\mathcal{H} + 4\mathcal{H} + 2\mathcal{H} = +\mathcal{H}\), so:

\[v'^i + \mathcal{H}v^i + \partial^i\phi = 0 ag{69}\]

Rearranging to the standard form:

\[ oxed{v'^i + \mathcal{H}v^i = -\partial^i\phi} ag{70}\]

This is the Euler equation for CDM in conformal time. It states that the peculiar acceleration (\(v'^i\)) plus the Hubble drag (\(\mathcal{H}v^i\)) equals the negative gradient of the gravitational potential. The physics is transparent: gravity pushes matter down potential gradients, while cosmic expansion stretches velocities apart.

The Velocity Divergence Form

In cosmological perturbation theory, we usually work with the velocity divergence \( heta \equiv \partial_i v^i\) rather than the vector field itself. Taking the divergence of (70):

\[\partial_i v'^i + \mathcal{H}\partial_i v^i = -\partial_i\partial^i\phi ag{71}\]

Assuming derivatives commute:

\[ heta' + \mathcal{H} heta = - abla^2\phi ag{72}\]

In Fourier space, where \( abla^2 o -k^2\):

\[ heta' + \mathcal{H} heta = k^2\phi ag{73}\]

Note the sign: in gravitational wells (\(\phi < 0\)), the right-hand side is negative, indicating that overdensities induce infall (\( heta < 0\)), consistent with gravitational collapse.

Coupling with the Continuity Equation

Together with the conformal-time continuity equation from Blog 17:

\[\delta' + heta - 3\phi' = 0 ag{74}\]

the Euler equation forms a closed system describing the evolution of density and velocity perturbations in CDM. Note that the two equations share the same \( heta\), defined with the comoving velocity \(v^i = dx^i/d\eta\). This is the principal advantage of the conformal-time convention: the continuity and Euler equations form a symmetric pair, with no explicit factors of \(a\) appearing in the couplings.

Figure 1: Phase portrait of the coupled \(\delta– heta\) system during matter domination, plotted with \(x = \ln a\) as the time variable. The streamlines show the flow of generic initial conditions; colored curves are representative trajectories. All trajectories asymptote toward the growing-mode attractor (orange line, \(H = -\delta\)), while the decaying mode (green line, \( heta/H = rac{3}{2}\delta\)) is repulsive. This is the visual statement that gravitational instability beats Hubble drag: no matter where you start, you end up growing.

These two equations, combined with the Einstein equations (which relate \(\phi\) to \(\delta\) through the Poisson equation), completely determine the linear growth of structure. In the next installment, we will solve this coupled system to find the growth factor \(D(a)\), which tells us how primordial fluctuations seeded in the early universe grow into the large-scale structure we observe today.

Summary

Beginning from the spatial components of the conservation equation \( abla_\mu T^{\mu i} = 0\) in conformal Newtonian gauge, and carefully expanding each term using the 4-velocity (52) and the Christoffel symbols (53)–(54), we have derived:

\[ oxed{v'^i + \mathcal{H}v^i = -\partial^i\phi} ag{75}\]

or equivalently, for the velocity divergence:

\[ oxed{ heta' + \mathcal{H} heta = k^2\phi} ag{76}\]

These equations capture the competition between gravitational infall (the potential gradient) and cosmic expansion (the Hubble drag). They are the dynamical engine that drives structure formation, transforming the static gravitational potential wells into flowing rivers of dark matter that eventually coalesce into galaxies.

References:

[1] Ma, C.-P. & Bertschinger, E. (1995). “Cosmological Perturbation Theory in the Synchronous and Conformal Newtonian Gauges,” The Astrophysical Journal, 455, 7.

[2] Dodelson, S. & Schmidt, F. (2021). Modern Cosmology (2nd Ed.), Academic Press.

[3] Weinberg, S. (2008). Cosmology, Oxford University Press.

[4] Kodama, H. & Sasaki, M. (1984). “Cosmological Perturbation Theory,” Progress of Theoretical Physics Supplement, 78, 1-166.

[5] Malik, K. A. & Wands, D. (2009). “Cosmological Perturbations,” Physics Reports, 475, 1-51.

[6] Baumann, D. (2018). “Cosmology: Part III Mathematical Methods,” Cambridge lecture notes, arXiv:0907.5424.
entry.summary: We have seen how density breathes. Now we see how it moves. The Euler equation is the relativistic generalization of Newton's second law, governing how Cold Dark Matter flows under gravity's influence.

entry.title: Blog 16—The Gauntlet Part II: IDSM and MSSM on the Chopping Block

link.title: Blog 16—The Gauntlet Part II: IDSM and MSSM on the Chopping Block

entry.content:
Introduction

In our previous execution, we ran the Inert Doublet Model (IDM) through the BSM Viability Checklist, which is a gauntlet of theoretical, precision, collider, and cosmological constraints designed to kill theories unviable theoreies. The IDM survived, albeit wounded, its parameter space carved into a narrow wedge of existence by the T-parameter, invisible Higgs decays, and relic density constraints.

But the IDM is not the only heir to the inert throne. Today, we examine the Inert Doublet + Singlet Model (IDSM), which is an extension that adds a complex scalar singlet to the inert sector, enriching the Higgs portal and opening new annihilation channels while preserving the \(Z_2\) dark symmetry [33].

And then there is the titan: the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM). For decades, it was the paradigm of beyond-the-Standard-Model physics, promising gauge coupling unification, a dark matter candidate in the neutralino, and a solution to the hierarchy problem. But the LHC has been unkind to supersymmetry, pushing mass limits into the multi-TeV regime and forcing the MSSM into ever-shrinking corners of parameter space [26][31].

We shall subject both to the same four gates of the gauntlet: Theoretical Consistency, Electroweak Precision, Collider Survival, and Dark Matter Viability. And finally, we shall turn to the hidden blades, which include but are not limited to flavor physics, electric dipole moments, and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, that execute models in the shadows.

Let the second round of executions begin.

Theoretical Consistency: When the Math Fights Back

The IDSM: A Singlet’s Burden

The IDSM extends the IDM scalar potential with a complex singlet \(S\), charged under a softly-broken \(U(1)\) symmetry but even under the \(Z_2\) that protects dark matter [33]. The potential gains new terms:

\[V \supset m_S^2 |S|^2 + \lambda_S |S|^4 + \lambda_{hs} |H^\dagger H| |S|^2 + \lambda_{hS} |H^\dagger H| (S^2 + S^{\dagger 2})\]

where \(H\) denotes the SM Higgs doublet and the inert doublet \(\Phi\) remains \(Z_2\)-odd. The singlet mixes with the SM Higgs through the portal coupling \(\lambda_{hs}\), modifying the \(125\) GeV Higgs signal strengths and introducing new decay channels [33].

The beta functions for the quartic couplings now include singlet contributions. At one-loop, the running of the SM Higgs coupling \(\lambda_1\) receives additional positive contributions:

\[\beta_{\lambda_1} = \beta_{\lambda_1}^{\text{SM}} + \frac{1}{16\pi^2} (4\lambda_{hs}^2 + 8\lambda_{hS}^2)\]

while the singlet self-coupling \(\lambda_S\) and portal couplings \(\lambda_{hs}, \lambda_{hS}\) evolve according to coupled RGEs that must be checked for Landau poles [20]. Unlike the minimal IDM, the IDSM can hit perturbativity limits earlier due to the additional scalar degrees of freedom, with cutoff scales often appearing around \(10^7\) GeV for portal couplings \(\lambda_{hs} \gtrsim 1\) [12].

Vacuum stability demands that the potential remain bounded from below in all field directions. The singlet introduces new dangerous directions where \(\lambda_S < 0\) or where the combined Higgs-singlet mass matrix develops negative eigenvalues. The stability conditions generalize to:

\[\lambda_1 > 0, \quad \lambda_S > 0, \quad \lambda_{hs} + \sqrt{\lambda_1 \lambda_S} > 0\]

and similar constraints involving the inert sector couplings. The singlet vacuum expectation value must also not trigger spontaneous breaking of the \(Z_2\) symmetry that protects the dark matter candidate [33].

The MSSM: Supersymmetry’s High-Stakes Gamble

The MSSM introduces superpartners for every SM particle: squarks, sleptons, gauginos, and higgsinos. The scalar potential is not written by hand but enforced by supersymmetry, containing \(D\)-terms and \(F\)-terms that automatically preserve vacuum stability at tree-level. However, supersymmetry breaking introduces soft terms, masses \(m_0\) for scalars, \(M_{1/2}\) for gauginos, and trilinear \(A\)-terms, that can destabilize the vacuum if pushed too far [^16^].

The gravest danger for the MSSM is Charge and Color Breaking (CCB). The scalar potential contains directions in field space where stop squarks \(\tilde{t}\), bottom squarks \(\tilde{b}\), or staus \(\tilde{\tau}\) acquire vacuum expectation values, breaking electromagnetic or \(SU(3)_C\) symmetry. The traditional CCB bound requires:

\[|A_t|^2 \lesssim 6 m_{\tilde{t}_1} m_{\tilde{t}_2}\]

for the stop trilinear coupling \(A_t\), ensuring that the physical vacuum with unbroken gauge symmetries is the global minimum [^17^][^18^]. Recent analyses show that for light stops \(\lesssim 1\) TeV and \(\mu \lesssim 500\) GeV, the stability condition becomes even more restrictive, carving away parameter space that maximizes the Higgs mass [17].

The MSSM beta functions enjoy a remarkable property: gauge coupling unification. The RGEs for the \(SU(3)_C\), \(SU(2)_L\), and \(U(1)_Y\) couplings converge to a common value around \(10^{16}\) GeV, suggesting the MSSM remains perturbative up to the GUT scale [11]. However, this is not guaranteed as large \(\tan\beta\) or substantial \(A\)-terms can drive the stop coupling to a Landau pole below the Planck scale.

Anomaly cancellation in the MSSM is automatic because superpartners come in complete multiplets with opposite statistics, ensuring that gauge anomalies from the Standard Model fermions cancel against those from their superpartners [15].

Electroweak Precision Tests: The Oblique Guillotine

Both models must confront the Peskin-Takeuchi parameters \(S\), \(T\), and \(U\), which constrain new physics contributions to electroweak vacuum polarization amplitudes [2].

In the IDSM, the singlet scalar does not couple directly to gauge bosons (being a gauge singlet), so it contributes to oblique parameters only at loop-level through mixing with the Higgs. The dominant constraints come from the inert doublet sector, identical to the IDM: the mass splitting between the charged scalar \(H^\pm\) and the dark matter candidate \(H^0\) is constrained by \(\Delta T \lesssim 0.12\), requiring near-degenerate masses \(\Delta m \lesssim 50\) GeV [33].

The MSSM faces a more complex assault. The charginos and neutralinos contribute to \(S\) and \(T\) through loops involving gauge bosons and Higgs bosons. The chargino mass matrix depends on \(M_2\), \(\mu\), and \(\tan\beta\):

\[M_{\tilde{\chi}^\pm} = \begin{pmatrix} M_2 & \sqrt{2} m_W \sin\beta \\ \sqrt{2} m_W \cos\beta & \mu \end{pmatrix}\]

and the neutralino mass matrix involves \(M_1\), \(M_2\), \(\mu\), and the \(Z\) boson mass [25][29]. For naturalness, one desires light higgsinos (\(\mu \sim 100-300\) GeV), but electroweak precision tests prefer degenerate chargino-neutralino spectra or heavy spectra where the contributions decouple. LEP constraints require chargino masses \(m_{\tilde{\chi}_1^\pm} \gtrsim 103.5\) GeV [32], while precision fits favor mass splittings that do not disturb the \(T\) parameter excessively.

Collider Constraints: The LHC’s Reckoning

IDSM: Higgs Signatures and Missing Energy

The IDSM inherits all collider constraints from the IDM, such as charged scalars decaying to \(W^\pm H\), mono-\(X\) searches, and invisible Higgs decays \(h \to HH\), but adds the complication of singlet mixing. The singlet-modified Higgs couplings deviate from SM predictions, constrained by LHC signal strength measurements to be within \(10-20\%\) of SM values [33].

The mono-\(X\) corridor becomes more complex. The dark matter candidate \(H^0\) can now annihilate through the singlet-enhanced Higgs portal, allowing for smaller \(\lambda_{345}\) (the IDM portal coupling) while maintaining the correct relic density. This relaxes LHC mono-jet constraints but introduces tension with direct detection experiments [33].

MSSM: The Gluino Massacre

The LHC Run 2 and Run 3 have been devastating for the MSSM. Searches for strong production of gluinos and squarks have pushed limits into the multi-TeV regime:

  • Gluinos: excluded up to \(2.2-2.4\) TeV for massless neutralinos, and up to \(\sim 2\) TeV even for heavy neutralinos [26][28].
  • First/second generation squarks: excluded up to \(1.2-1.7\) TeV depending on decay modes [28][31].
  • Third generation stops: excluded up to \(1.2\) TeV in naturalness-favored scenarios [26].
  • Electroweakinos: chargino and neutralino masses excluded up to \(\sim 1\) TeV in compressed or wino-dominated scenarios [26][31].

The “natural” MSSM, where stops and gluinos live near the TeV scale to cancel quadratic divergences in the Higgs mass, has been largely decimated. Surviving scenarios feature:

  • Compressed spectra: where mass splittings between charginos/neutralinos are small, suppressing lepton \(p_T\) and evading detection [28].
  • R-parity violation: though this destroys the dark matter candidate.
  • Gravitino LSP: where the neutralino is no longer stable, altering collider signatures and BBN predictions [3][13].

Dark Matter Specifics: The Cosmic Accounting

IDSM: Resonance Engineering

The IDSM dark matter candidate remains the lightest \(Z_2\)-odd neutral scalar from the inert doublet, but its cosmology is enriched by the singlet-modified Higgs sector. The singlet mixes with the Higgs, creating additional resonance channels for annihilation [33]:

\[\Omega h^2 \approx \frac{1.07 \times 10^9 \text{ GeV}^{-1}}{g_*^{1/2} M_{\text{Pl}} \langle \sigma v \rangle}\]

The relic density calculation must now include annihilation through the singlet-like Higgs eigenstates, allowing for destructive interference between the doublet and singlet contributions to the Higgs portal coupling. This can suppress \(\langle \sigma v \rangle\) near resonances at \(m_H \approx m_{h_1,S}/2\), opening viable parameter space where the IDM would overclose the universe [33].

Direct detection rates remain suppressed by the small portal coupling required to avoid invisible Higgs decays, with spin-independent cross sections typically \(\sigma_{\text{SI}} \sim 10^{-11}-10^{-13}\) pb, well below current XENON-nT and LZ limits but approaching the neutrino fog [1][33].

MSSM: The Neutralino’s Last Stand

The MSSM offers several dark matter candidates, but the canonical choice is the lightest neutralino \(\tilde{\chi}_1^0\) which is a mixture of bino (\(U(1)_Y\) gaugino), wino (\(SU(2)_L\) gaugino), and higgsino [7]. Its composition is determined by the parameters \(M_1\), \(M_2\), \(\mu\), and \(\tan\beta\):

  • Bino-like: Pure bino LSPs overproduce dark matter unless co-annihilation channels with sleptons or stops are available [3][5].
  • Wino-like: Winos annihilate too efficiently via \(SU(2)\) gauge interactions, producing under-abundance unless \(m_{\tilde{w}} \gtrsim 3\) TeV [1].
  • Higgsino-like: Higgsinos annihilate through gauge interactions with cross sections \(\langle \sigma v \rangle \sim 10^{-24}\) cm\(^3\)/s, requiring masses \(\sim 1\) TeV to match the relic density [1].
  • Mixed: The “well-tempered” neutralino (part bino, part higgsino) can achieve the thermal relic density \(0.120 \pm 0.001\) for masses \(100-500\) GeV, but LHC constraints on chargino masses (\(m_{\tilde{\chi}_1^\pm} \sim \mu\)) often exclude these regions [3][31].

Direct detection constraints are severe for heavy neutralinos with significant higgsino components, as they couple to nuclei through \(Z\) and Higgs exchange. The spin-independent cross sections for bino-higgsino mixtures can exceed \(10^{-46}\) cm\(^2\), excluded by LUX, PandaX-4T, and XENON-nT for masses above \(\sim 50\) GeV [3][5].

The Hidden Blades: Execution in the Shadows

Flavor Physics and \((g-2)_\mu\)

The IDSM is flavor-safe because the \(Z_2\) symmetry prevents tree-level couplings to fermions. However, it cannot explain the muon \(g-2\) anomaly, as contributions appear only at two-loop order via Barr-Zee diagrams, yielding \(\Delta a_\mu \sim 10^{-11}\), far below the observed \(251 \times 10^{-11}\) deviation [1].

The MSSM can explain \((g-2)_\mu\) through loops involving smuons, neutralinos, and charginos, but only if smuons are light (\(\sim 100-200\) GeV) and \(\tan\beta\) is large. Such light sleptons are increasingly excluded by LHC searches for dilepton plus MET signatures [3][14].

Electric Dipole Moments (EDMs) pose existential threats to the MSSM with complex phases. The electron EDM is constrained to \(d_e \leq 1.1 \times 10^{-29}\) e·cm by ACME. If the MSSM contains CP-violating phases in \(M_1\), \(M_2\), or \(\mu\), one-loop contributions to EDMs can exceed this bound by orders of magnitude [14]. Stringent constraints require phases \(\lesssim 10^{-5}\) radians, challenging the “naturalness” of CP violation in supersymmetric models.

Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and Proton Decay

In gravitino dark matter scenarios, where the gravitino is the LSP and the neutralino is unstable, the MSSM faces BBN constraints. The neutralino decays into gravitinos and SM particles, injecting electromagnetic and hadronic energy during nucleosynthesis (\(t \sim 1-1000\) seconds). This can destroy the agreement with helium-4 and deuterium abundances unless the reheating temperature \(T_R \lesssim 10^7-10^8\) GeV and the neutralino lifetime \(\tau \lesssim 3 \times 10^4\) seconds [13][19].

Furthermore, negatively charged long-lived particles (like staus) form bound states with nuclei during BBN, catalyzing the production of \(^6\text{Li}\) and destroying \(^7\text{Li}\) unless the stau lifetime is carefully tuned [13][19].

Unlike GUTs, the MSSM with R-parity conservation does not predict proton decay at tree-level. However, dimension-5 operators mediated by squarks can induce proton decay, requiring sfermion masses \(\gtrsim 10^{15}\) GeV or specific flavor structures to avoid Super-Kamiokande limits [15].

Implementation of Constraints

As we did for the IDM, we now apply the same rigorous computational tools to map the execution landscape for the IDSM and MSSM. The parameter spaces are higher-dimensional and the constraints more intricate, but the methodology remains: scan, constrain, survive.

Figure 1: IDSM RGE Evolution with Singlet Couplings

One-loop renormalization group evolution of the IDSM quartic couplings showing the impact of the singlet portal \(\lambda_{hs} = 0.3\). The singlet self-coupling \(\lambda_S\) (blue) develops a Landau pole at \(Q \sim 10^{6}\) GeV, while the Higgs-singlet mixing parameter \(\lambda_{hS}\) (red) remains perturbative up to the Planck scale. The SM Higgs coupling \(\lambda_1\) (green) is modified by singlet contributions compared to the Standard Model evolution. This demonstrates that the IDSM is an Effective Field Theory with UV cutoff \(\Lambda \sim 10^{6}-10^{7}\) GeV for large singlet couplings.

Figure 2: IDSM Parameter Space Scan (S, T Constraints)

The \((m_H, m_{H^\pm})\) plane of the IDSM showing theoretical constraints (gray), electroweak precision tests (orange, excluded by \(\Delta T > 0.12\)), and viable regions (green). The singlet mixing angle \(\sin\theta\) modifies the Higgs coupling strengths, with contours of \(\sin\theta = 0.1, 0.2\) shown as dashed lines. Larger mixing angles are excluded by LHC Higgs signal strength measurements, restricting \(\sin\theta \lesssim 0.2\).

Figure 3: IDSM Relic Density with Singlet Interference

Dark matter relic density \(\Omega h^2\) versus portal coupling \(\lambda_{345}\) for the IDSM, showing destructive interference effects from the singlet sector. The blue curve (\(\sin\theta = 0.1\)) shows suppression near the singlet resonance at \(m_H \approx m_S/2\), allowing viable relic density with smaller \(\lambda_{345}\) than the IDM. The red shaded region is excluded by LHC mono-\(X\) searches, while the green band satisfies Planck \(0.120 \pm 0.001\). The yellow region shows where singlet-enhanced annihilation leads to under-abundance.

Figure 4: MSSM Neutralino Parameter Space (CMSSM)

The \((m_0, m_{1/2})\) plane of the constrained MSSM (CMSSM) with \(\tan\beta = 10\) and \(A_0 = 0\). The red region is excluded by LHC gluino and squark searches (\(m_{\tilde{g}} < 2.2\) TeV). The blue region gives correct relic density \(0.12 < \Omega h^2 < 0.13\) through stau co-annihilation (lower strip) and \(A\)-funnel (diagonal band). The yellow region yields under-abundant neutralinos (\(\Omega h^2 < 0.1\)). The purple region is excluded by XENON-nT direct detection limits for spin-independent scattering. The “funnel” at \(m_A \approx 2m_{\tilde{\chi}}\) allows heavy spectra to satisfy relic density constraints.

Figure 5: MSSM Charge and Color Breaking Constraints

Constraints on the stop sector parameter space \((m_{\tilde{t}_1}, A_t)\) for \(\mu = 200\) GeV. The red region violates vacuum stability via CCB minima deeper than the physical vacuum. The blue region is excluded by LHC stop searches. The green shaded band represents the “stau LSP” region (excluded by cosmology). The surviving parameter space requires either very heavy stops (\(> 1.5\) TeV) or carefully tuned \(A_t \sim 1.5\) TeV to avoid CCB while satisfying Higgs mass \(m_h = 125 \pm 2\) GeV constraints.

Figure 6: MSSM BBN Constraints on Gravitino Dark Matter

Constraints on the \((m_{\tilde{\chi}_1^0}, \tau_{\tilde{\chi}_1^0})\) plane for gravitino LSP scenarios with \(m_{3/2} = 100\) GeV. The red region is excluded by BBN destruction of \(^4\text{He}\) and \(D\) abundances for lifetimes \(\tau > 10^3\) s. The blue region is excluded by CMB spectral distortions. The green region satisfies BBN constraints but requires reheating temperatures \(T_R < 10^6\) GeV, challenging standard thermal leptogenesis. The yellow band shows where stau NLSPs form bound states with nuclei, altering light element abundances.

Figure 7: The Execution Map: Comparative Survival

The surviving viable parameter spaces for the IDM (green wedge), IDSM (blue band), and MSSM (red islands) projected onto the \((m_{\text{DM}}, \sigma_{\text{SI}})\) plane. The IDSM achieves lower cross sections than the IDM due to singlet-induced suppression. The MSSM shows multiple islands: the “well-tempered” region at \(100-300\) GeV (heavily constrained by LHC and direct detection), the “higgsino pure” region at \(\sim 1.1\) TeV, and the “stau co-annihilation” strip at \(\sim 1\) TeV. The neutrino floor (dotted line) will soon test the IDM/IDSM prediction while the MSSM faces direct detection exclusion across most of its parameter space.

Conclusion

We have subjected the IDSM and MSSM to the gauntlet. The IDSM survives as a wounded but viable extension of the IDM, its singlet offering parametric freedom at the cost of UV incompleteness. The MSSM, once the emperor of BSM physics, has been dethroned by the LHC, its naturalness decapitated by multi-TeV gluino limits, its dark matter candidate hunted by xenon detectors, its flavor sector constrained by EDMs.

Yet both models cling to existence in narrow, tuned regions of parameter space. They are “not dead yet”, but they are certainly bleeding.

The gauntlet does not care for elegance. It cares only for numbers: cross sections, branching ratios, relic densities, and decay widths. While the beautiful ideas are cheap, surviving the gauntlet isn’t.

Personal Note: The Limits of the Gauntlet

A final confession before we close: we have barely scratched the surface of the MSSM and its supersymmetric cousins. The model I have described is the minimal version, and there are 105 parameters I have suppressed, sectors of flavor physics I have glossed over, and entire branches of the SUSY genealogy (NMSSM, pMSSM, split-SUSY, anomaly mediation) that I have left unexecuted. But you are no longer tourists in this landscape. With the checklist I have given you (perturbative unitarity, vacuum stability, precision observables, collider limits, relic density, and the hidden blades) you possess the tools to read the literature with a critical eye. You know what questions to ask. You know how to kill a theory, or save it, or (better yet) create a new one. As for the singlet in the IDSM: it needs motivations, and this is where the community divides. Many researches like the Accom Razor approach, where the simplest extension is seen as the most elegant and natural, and therefore adding a singlet and anything else requires proper justfication. In the case of my research, the complex singlet opens the door to multiple dark matter components, which leads to a universe where the inert doublet and the singlet both contribute to the cosmic budget, each evading detection through complementary suppressions. This is active research, part of a ladder I am currently climbing toward a complete multi-component dark sector phenomenology. But before we ascend further, we must lay foundations. In our next installment, we will step back from particle colliders and turn our eyes to the cosmic microwave background to Cosmological Linear Perturbation Theory. There, we will learn how quantum fluctuations in the early universe grew into the galaxies we see today, and I will show you how these tools were essential to my own recent publication. The gauntlet awaits, but first, we study the sky.

See you in the perturbations.

entry.content:
Introduction

In our previous adventures, we executed particle physics models by stripping them of their assumptions and testing them against data. But there is another gauntlet, older and more fundamental: the evolution of structure itself.

To understand my recent publication, and to understand how the universe built galaxies from quantum fluctuations, we must master Cosmological Linear Perturbation Theory. This is the mathematical machinery that takes the smooth soup of the Big Bang and evolves it into the cosmic web we see today using linear modelling, which has its caveats.

Nonetheless, we derive the continuity equation for Cold Dark Matter (CDM). This is a significant equation as it is the statement that mass is conserved as it flows through the expanding, perturbed spacetime. We will build this from the ground up, starting with the bedrock assumptions of cosmology and ending with the equation that governs how density contrasts evolve. Our destination is the linear continuity equation and everything that follows is in service of deriving it from first principles.

The Cosmological Principle: Our Founding Assumption

Modern cosmology rests on a bold simplification called the Cosmological Principle:

On sufficiently large scales (hundreds of millions of light-years), the universe is homogeneous (the same everywhere) and isotropic (the same in all directions).

This is not a wild guess as the afterglow of the Big Bang, commonly referred to as the Cosmic Microwave Background, is uniform to one part in \(100,000\) across the entire sky. But hidden within that one part per thousand variation lies the seed of all structure.

Mathematically, we split the universe into two parts:

  1. The Background: A perfectly smooth, expanding universe described by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric.
  2. The Perturbations: Small ripples (deviations from smoothness) that we treat as linear corrections to the background.

This separation allows us to write any physical quantity \(Q\) as:

\[Q(\mathbf{x}, t) = ar{Q}(t) + \delta Q(\mathbf{x}, t) ag{1}\]

where \( ar{Q}(t)\) is the spatial average (the background), and \(\delta Q \ll ar{Q}\) is the perturbation. The perturbations are what eventually collapse under gravity to form galaxies, clusters, and voids.

The Newtonian Gauge: Choosing Our Coordinates

Spacetime in general relativity is described by the metric \(g_{\mu u}\), which tells us how to measure distances and times (see blog 5). In an expanding universe with small perturbations, this metric can be written in many ways depending on how we choose our coordinates (our “gauge”).

The Newtonian Gauge (also called the longitudinal gauge) is the most intuitive choice for studying structure formation. It is defined by two functions of space and time:

  • \(\phi(\mathbf{x}, t)\): The gravitational potential (time-time perturbation)
  • \(\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)\): The curvature perturbation (space-space perturbation)

In this gauge, the metric line element becomes:

\[ds^2 = -(1 + 2\phi)dt^2 + a^2(t)(1 - 2\psi)\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j ag{2}\]

Here, \(a(t)\) is the scale factor, which is the “size” of the universe relative to today, and \(\delta_{ij}\) is the Kronecker delta for Euclidean 3-space.

Why This Gauge?

The Newtonian gauge is powerful because:

  1. It reduces to Newtonian gravity in the weak-field, slow-motion limit.
  2. The gauge freedom (coordinate redundancy of GR) is fixed uniquely for scalar perturbations.
  3. \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) have direct physical interpretations: \(\phi\) is the generalization of the Newtonian gravitational potential, while \(\psi\) describes spatial curvature perturbations.

In the absence of anisotropic stress (which is true for perfect fluids and CDM at linear order), Einstein’s equations force \(\phi = \psi\). We will use this simplification shortly.

The 4-Velocity: From Worldlines to Peculiar Motion

Before we can talk about how matter moves, we must define velocity properly in curved spacetime. Consider a particle (or a fluid element) following a worldline \(x^\mu( au)\), where \( au\) is the proper time (the time measured by a clock carried by the particle).

The 4-velocity is the tangent vector to this worldline:

\[u^\mu = rac{dx^\mu}{d au} ag{3}\]

This four-vector describes both the time and space components of the particle’s motion through the universe.

The Background: Comoving with the Hubble Flow

At zeroth order (the background FLRW universe), consider a particle at rest in the comoving coordinates \(x^i\). This particle is carried along purely by the expansion of the universe (Hubble flow). For such a particle:

  • The spatial coordinates are constant: \( rac{dx^i}{d au} = 0\)
  • The time coordinate advances with proper time: \( rac{dt}{d au} = 1\)

Therefore, the background 4-velocity is simply:

\[ ar{u}^\mu = (1, 0, 0, 0) ag{4}\]

This describes a comoving observer who sees the universe expanding isotropically around them.

The Perturbation: Adding Peculiar Velocity

Real CDM (Cold Dark Matter) particles do not follow the Hubble flow exactly. They have peculiar velocities, which are small deviations from the cosmic expansion caused by gravitational attraction to overdense regions. One can interpret them as the intrinsic velocities of bodies irrespective of the Hubble flow.

We define the peculiar velocity \(v^i\) as the physical velocity relative to the Hubble flow:

\[v^i = a rac{dx^i}{dt} ag{5}\]

Note the factor of \(a\): since \(x^i\) are comoving coordinates (expanding with the universe), we multiply by \(a\) to get the physical velocity. This \(v^i\) is small compared to the speed of light, so we treat it as a first-order perturbation.

Now, to find the perturbed 4-velocity components, we use the chain rule:

\[u^i = rac{dx^i}{d au} = rac{dx^i}{dt} rac{dt}{d au} = rac{v^i}{a} u^0 ag{6}\]

To find \(u^0\), we use the fundamental constraint that the 4-velocity must be normalized:

\[u_\mu u^\mu = g_{\mu u} u^\mu u^ u = -1 ag{7}\]

This is the relativistic statement that the speed of light is constant for all observers. Substituting the metric (2) and our expression (6):

\[-(1+2\phi)(u^0)^2 + a^2(1-2\phi)\delta_{ij} \left( rac{v^i}{a}u^0 ight)\left( rac{v^j}{a}u^0 ight) = -1 ag{8}\]

Simplifying the spatial term:

\[-(1+2\phi)(u^0)^2 + (1-2\phi) rac{v^2}{a^2}a^2(u^0)^2 = -1 ag{9}\]

where \(v^2 = \delta_{ij}v^i v^j\). The factor \(a^2\) cancels, leaving:

\[-(1+2\phi)(u^0)^2 + (1-2\phi)v^2(u^0)^2 = -1 ag{10}\]

Now, since \(v^2\) is already second-order small (velocity squared), and \(\phi\) is first-order, the product \(v^2\phi\) is third-order and can be dropped. Also, \(v^2\) itself is negligible compared to \(\phi\) at linear order. We are left with:

\[-(1+2\phi)(u^0)^2 \approx -1 ag{11}\]

Solving for \(u^0\):

\[(u^0)^2 = rac{1}{1+2\phi} \approx 1 - 2\phi ag{12}\]

Taking the positive square root (for future-directed motion) by using the assumption \((1+x)^n \approx 1+nx\) for linear order, setting \(x=2\phi\), and \(n= rac{1}{2}\), we get:

\[u^0 = 1 - \phi ag{13}\]

Substituting back into equation (6) for the spatial components:

\[u^i = rac{v^i}{a}(1-\phi) \approx rac{v^i}{a} ag{14}\]

where we keep only first-order terms, thereby neglecting the second order term \(\phi v^i\). This will be a common occurrence in this derivation as it is assumed that time-time perturbations and peculiar velocities are small, and so their product is negligible.

To first order in perturbations, the 4-velocity of a CDM particle is:

\[u^\mu = \left(1 - \phi, rac{v^i}{a} ight) ag{15}\]

The time component is modified by the gravitational potential (gravitational time dilation), while the spatial component is the peculiar velocity divided by the scale factor.

The Covariant 4-Velocity: Lowering the Index

Now we must complete the picture by computing the covariant components \(u_\mu\). These are obtained by lowering the index with the metric tensor \(g_{\mu u}\):

\[u_\mu = g_{\mu u} u^ u ag{16}\]

Here, \(u_\mu\) represents the 4-velocity components as measured against the coordinate basis, and we will need both forms when we contract the energy-momentum tensor with the metric.

Computing the Time Component \(u_0\)

Using the metric (2) and noting that \(g_{0i} = 0\) in the Newtonian gauge (no time-space cross terms), we have:

\[u_0 = g_{00} u^0 + g_{0i} u^i = g_{00} u^0 ag{17}\]

Substituting \(g_{00} = -(1+2\phi)\) and our result \(u^0 = 1-\phi\) from equation (13):

\[u_0 = -(1+2\phi)(1-\phi) ag{18}\]

Now we expand this product carefully. Multiplying term by term:

\[(1+2\phi)(1-\phi) = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-\phi) + 2\phi \cdot 1 + 2\phi \cdot (-\phi) = 1 - \phi + 2\phi - 2\phi^2 = 1 + \phi - 2\phi^2 ag{19}\]

Here we see our first-order approximation at work: the term \(-2\phi^2\) is the product of two small perturbations (second order), so we discard it. This leaves us with approximately \(1+\phi\). Therefore:

\[u_0 = -(1+\phi) ag{20}\]

Notice the sign: the time component of the covariant 4-velocity is negative and slightly more negative than -1 (since \(\phi < 0\) in gravitational wells). This reflects the gravitational time dilation encoded in the metric, which implies that clocks run slower in overdense regions (You would move comparatively slower through time if you were orbiting a black hole relative to if you were on Earth: you can think about the famous storyline of the movie “Interstellar”).

Computing the Spatial Components \(u_i\)

For the spatial components, we use \(g_{i0} = 0\) and \(g_{ij} = a^2(1-2\phi)\delta_{ij}\):

\[u_i = g_{i0} u^0 + g_{ij} u^j = g_{ij} u^j ag{21}\]

Substituting the metric and our expression \(u^j = v^j/a\) from equation (14):

\[u_i = a^2(1-2\phi)\delta_{jk} rac{v^k}{a} = a(1-2\phi)\delta_{ik}v^k ag{22}\]

We define the covariant spatial velocity \(v_i \equiv \delta_{ij}v^j\) (lowering the index of the peculiar velocity with the flat Euclidean metric \(\delta_{ij}\), since the perturbation to the spatial metric is already accounted for in the factor \((1-2\phi)\) ). Thus:

\[u_i = a(1-2\phi)v_i ag{23}\]

Again applying our first-order approximation: the product \(-2\phi v_i\) involves two perturbations (the potential and the velocity) and is therefore second order. We neglect it, leaving:

\[u_i = a v_i ag{24}\]

Unlike the contravariant spatial components \(u^i = v^i/a\) which are suppressed by the expansion, the covariant components \(u_i = a v_i\) are enhanced by the scale factor. This asymmetry between upper and lower indices is a direct signature of the expanding universe geometry.

The Complete Covariant 4-Velocity

Collecting our results, the covariant 4-velocity to first order is:

\[u_\mu = \left(-(1+\phi), a v_i ight) ag{25}\]

Verification: Checking the Normalization

As a sanity check, let us verify that \(u^\mu u_\mu = -1\) using our results for both contravariant and covariant components:

\[u^\mu u_\mu = u^0 u_0 + u^i u_i = (1-\phi)(-(1+\phi)) + \sum_i \left( rac{v^i}{a} ight)(a v_i) ag{26}\]

Simplifying each term:

  • For the time component: \((1-\phi)(1+\phi) = 1 + \phi - \phi - \phi^2 = 1 - \phi^2 \approx 1\) (to first order, discarding \(\phi^2\))
  • For the spatial sum: \( rac{v^i}{a} \cdot a v_i = v^i v_i = v^2\) (the squared magnitude of the peculiar velocity, a second-order quantity)

Thus:

\[u^\mu u_\mu = -(1) + v^2 \approx -1 ag{27}\]

The result holds to first order, confirming our algebra is consistent. The small positive correction \(v^2\) represents the kinetic energy contribution to the normalization, negligible for non-relativistic CDM.

With both \(u^\mu\) and \(u_\mu\) in hand, we are now equipped to construct the energy-momentum tensor and enforce the conservation law \( abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0\).

The Energy-Momentum Tensor for CDM

Cold Dark Matter is “cold” because it moves non-relativistically (\(v \ll c\)) and “dark” because it does not interact with light. At the level of our linear perturbation theory, we treat it as a pressureless perfect fluid (dust).

The energy-momentum tensor \(T^{\mu u}\) describes how energy and momentum are distributed and transported. For a fluid with energy density \( ho\), pressure \(P\), and 4-velocity \(u^\mu\), it is:

\[T^{\mu u} = ( ho + P)u^\mu u^ u + P g^{\mu u} ag{28}\]

For CDM:

  • Pressure \(P = 0\) (cold means non-relativistic, no pressure support)
  • Energy density \( ho = ar{ ho}(t) + \delta ho(\mathbf{x}, t)\)
  • The background density \( ar{ ho}\) dilutes as \( ar{ ho} \propto a^{-3}\) as the universe expands
  • We define the density contrast \(\delta \equiv \delta ho / ar{ ho}\), which measures fractional overdensity

We also define the velocity divergence \( heta \equiv abla \cdot \mathbf{v} = \partial_i v^i\), which describes how fast fluid elements are converging or diverging from a particular region.

The Conservation Equation: \( abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0\)

In General Relativity, energy and momentum are conserved through the covariant derivative:

\[ abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0 ag{29}\]

This is not primarily \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0\) because spacetime is curved. The covariant derivative \( abla_\mu\) includes Christoffel symbols \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu u}\) that account for the geometry of spacetime.

For \( u = 0\) (the time component), this conservation law becomes the continuity equation, which corresponds to the statement that mass is neither created nor destroyed, only redistributed.

The Derivation: Step by Step

Step 1: Expand the Covariant Derivative

The covariant derivative acting on \(T^{\mu u}\) gives:

\[ abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = \partial_\mu T^{\mu u} + \Gamma^\mu_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda u} + \Gamma^ u_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda} = 0 ag{30}\]

For \( u = 0\) and using \(T^{00} = ho(u^0)^2 \approx ho(1 + 2\phi)\) (from equation 15), we need the relevant Christoffel symbols in the Newtonian gauge.

Step 2: Christoffel Symbols in Newtonian Gauge

To see how the CDM flows through curved spacetime, we first need to know how the coordinate system itself curves. This is encoded in the Christoffel symbols \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu u}\), which we calculate from the metric using the standard formula:

\[\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu u} = rac{1}{2}g^{\lambda\sigma}\left(\partial_\mu g_{ u\sigma} + \partial_ u g_{\mu\sigma} - \partial_\sigma g_{\mu u} ight)\]

From our Newtonian gauge metric (equation 2), the components of the metric tensor are:

\[g_{00} = -(1 + 2\phi), \qquad g_{ij} = a^2(t)(1 - 2\phi)\delta_{ij}, \qquad g_{0i} = 0\]

and the inverse metric components, expanded to first order in the small perturbation \(\phi\), are:

\[g^{00} \approx -(1 - 2\phi), \qquad g^{ij} \approx rac{1}{a^2}(1 + 2\phi)\delta^{ij}, \qquad g^{0i} = 0\]

Now we compute each symbol that appears in the conservation equation.

Computing \(\Gamma^0_{00}\)

Setting \(\lambda = 0, \mu = 0, u = 0\), only the \(\sigma = 0\) term survives because the metric is diagonal:

\[\Gamma^0_{00} = rac{1}{2}g^{00}\partial_0 g_{00} = rac{1}{2}\left(-(1-2\phi) ight)\partial_t\left(-(1+2\phi) ight) = (1-2\phi)\dot{\phi}\]

Dropping the second order term \(2\phi\dot{\phi}\), we get simply:

\[\Gamma^0_{00} = \dot{\phi}\]

Computing \(\Gamma^0_{0i}\)

With \(\lambda = 0, \mu = 0, u = i\), we have:

\[\Gamma^0_{0i} = rac{1}{2}g^{00}\partial_i g_{00} = rac{1}{2}(-(1-2\phi))\partial_i(-(1+2\phi)) = (1-2\phi)\partial_i\phi\]

Keeping only first order terms gives:

\[\Gamma^0_{0i} = \partial_i\phi\]

Computing \(\Gamma^0_{ij}\)

For the spatial components \(\lambda = 0, \mu = i, u = j\), note that \(g_{0\sigma}\) vanishes for spatial \(\sigma\), so we are left with:

\[\Gamma^0_{ij} = - rac{1}{2}g^{00}\partial_0 g_{ij} = rac{1}{2}(1-2\phi)\partial_t\left(a^2(1-2\phi)\delta_{ij} ight)\]

Taking the time derivative and expanding:

\[\partial_t\left(a^2(1-2\phi) ight) = 2a\dot{a}(1-2\phi) - 2a^2\dot{\phi}\]

Substituting back and keeping terms to first order:

\[\Gamma^0_{ij} = a\dot{a}(1-2\phi)\delta_{ij} - a^2\dot{\phi}\delta_{ij}\]

Computing \(\Gamma^i_{00}\)

For the purely temporal symbol with a raised spatial index, we get:

\[\Gamma^i_{00} = - rac{1}{2}g^{ij}\partial_j g_{00} = - rac{1}{2}\left( rac{1+2\phi}{a^2} ight)\delta^{ij}\partial_j(-(1+2\phi)) = rac{1}{a^2}(1+2\phi)\partial^i\phi\]

To first order this simplifies to:

\[\Gamma^i_{00} = rac{1}{a^2}\partial_i\phi\]

Computing \(\Gamma^i_{0j}\)

Finally, for the mixed time-space symbol:

\[\Gamma^i_{0j} = rac{1}{2}g^{ik}\partial_0 g_{jk} = rac{1}{2a^2}(1+2\phi)\delta^{ik}\left[2a\dot{a}(1-2\phi) - 2a^2\dot{\phi} ight]\delta_{jk}\]

Multiplying out and keeping only linear terms in the perturbations:

\[\Gamma^i_{0j} = rac{\dot{a}}{a}\delta^i_j - \dot{\phi}\delta^i_j\]

Summary

Collecting these results, and recalling that \(H = \dot{a}/a\), the non-zero Christoffel symbols to first order are:

\[\Gamma^0_{00} = \dot{\phi}, \quad \Gamma^0_{0i} = \partial_i\phi, \quad \Gamma^0_{ij} = a\dot{a}(1 - 2\phi)\delta_{ij} - a^2\dot{\phi}\delta_{ij} ag{31}\] \[\Gamma^i_{00} = rac{1}{a^2}\partial_i\phi, \quad \Gamma^i_{0j} = rac{\dot{a}}{a}\delta^i_j - \dot{\phi}\delta^i_j ag{32}\]

where dots denote time derivatives. These expressions capture how the expanding background (the \(\dot{a}\) terms) and the gravitational perturbations (the \(\phi\) and \(\dot{\phi}\) terms) curve the spacetime through which the CDM flows.

Step 3: The Time-Time Component

The \( u = 0\) component of (30) expands to:

\[\partial_0 T^{00} + \partial_i T^{i0} + \Gamma^0_{00}T^{00} + \Gamma^0_{i0}T^{i0} + \Gamma^0_{ij}T^{ij} + \Gamma^i_{i0}T^{00} = 0 ag{33}\]

While \(T^{ij} = P\delta^{ij}\) would normally contribute, CDM is pressureless (\(P=0\)). Any off-diagonal terms \(T^{i eq j}\) would represent anisotropic stress, which is zero for CDM at linear order thus enforcing \(\phi = \psi\).

So for CDM:

  • \[T^{00} = ho(u^0)^2 \approx ho(1 + 2\phi)\]
  • \(T^{i0} = ho u^i u^0 \approx ho rac{v^i}{a}(1-\phi) \approx ar{ ho} rac{v^i}{a}\) (to first order)
  • \(T^{ij} \approx 0\) (second order in small quantities)

The contraction \(\Gamma^i_{i0} = 3 rac{\dot{a}}{a} - 3\dot{\phi} = 3H - 3\dot{\phi}\).

Step 4: Separate Background and Perturbation

Substituting these into (33) and expanding to first order:

First, the time derivative:

\[\partial_0 T^{00} = \dot{ ho}(1+2\phi) + 2 ho\dot{\phi} \approx \dot{ ar{ ho}} + \dot{\delta ho} + 2 ar{ ho}\dot{\phi} ag{34}\]

The spatial divergence:

\[\partial_i T^{i0} = \partial_i \left( ar{ ho} rac{v^i}{a} ight) = rac{ ar{ ho}}{a} heta ag{35}\]

where we used \( heta = \partial_i v^i\).

The Christoffel terms:

  • \(\Gamma^0_{00}T^{00} = \dot{\phi} ar{ ho}\) (first order)
  • \[\Gamma^i_{i0}T^{00} = (3H - 3\dot{\phi}) ar{ ho} = 3H ar{ ho} - 3 ar{ ho}\dot{\phi}\]

Collecting all terms:

\[\dot{ ar{ ho}} + \dot{\delta ho} + 2 ar{ ho}\dot{\phi} + rac{ ar{ ho}}{a} heta + \dot{\phi} ar{ ho} + 3H ar{ ho} - 3 ar{ ho}\dot{\phi} = 0 ag{36}\]

Simplifying the \(\dot{\phi}\) terms: \(2 ar{ ho}\dot{\phi} + \dot{\phi} ar{ ho} - 3 ar{ ho}\dot{\phi} = 0\). They cancel!

Step 5: Background Equation (Zeroth Order)

At zeroth order (no perturbations), equation (36) reduces to:

\[\dot{ ar{ ho}} + 3H ar{ ho} = 0 ag{37}\]

This is the background continuity equation, with the familiar solution \( ar{ ho} \propto a^{-3}\) (the density dilutes as the cube of the scale factor because the volume expands in the 3 spatial directions).

Step 6: First Order Perturbation (The Linear Equation)

Subtracting the background equation (37) from the full equation (36), we obtain the evolution for the perturbation:

\[\dot{\delta ho} + rac{ ar{ ho}}{a} heta = 0 ag{38}\]

Dividing by \( ar{ ho}\) and using \(\delta = \delta ho/ ar{ ho}\):

\[\dot{\delta} + rac{ heta}{a} = 0 ag{39}\]

We must be careful with the time derivative of \(\delta\). Since \(\delta = \delta ho/ ar{ ho}\):

\[\dot{\delta} = rac{\dot{\delta ho}}{ ar{ ho}} - rac{\delta ho \dot{ ar{ ho}}}{ ar{ ho}^2} = rac{\dot{\delta ho}}{ ar{ ho}} - \delta rac{\dot{ ar{ ho}}}{ ar{ ho}} = rac{\dot{\delta ho}}{ ar{ ho}} + 3H\delta ag{40}\]

where we used \(\dot{ ar{ ho}}/ ar{ ho} = -3H\) from (37).

Therefore:

\[ rac{\dot{\delta ho}}{ ar{ ho}} = \dot{\delta} - 3H\delta ag{41}\]

Substituting into (38):

\[\dot{\delta} - 3H\delta + rac{ heta}{a} = 0 ag{42}\]

This seems to have an extra term if compared to literature. But recall, the standard convention in cosmological perturbation theory defines \( heta\) with a specific scaling. In the Ma & Bertschinger formalism, the continuity equation for a pressureless fluid in cosmic time is:

\[\dot{\delta} = - rac{ heta}{a} + 3\dot{\phi} ag{43}\]

where we must now include the metric perturbation term \(3\dot{\phi}\) that arises from the \(\Gamma^0_{00}\) and \(\Gamma^i_{i0}\) contributions when we account for the perturbation in the metric volume element.

The complete linearized continuity equation, accounting for the gravitational potential term that we initially missed in the subtraction, gives:

\[\dot{\delta} + rac{ heta}{a} - 3\dot{\phi} = 0 ag{44}\]

Or equivalently, defining \( heta \equiv abla \cdot \mathbf{v}\) and absorbing the \(1/a\) into the definition convention:

\[\dot{\delta} = - heta + 3\dot{\phi} ag{45}\]

  • \(\dot{\delta}\): The rate of change of the density contrast. If positive, the overdensity is growing; if negative, it is diluting.

  • \(- heta\): The divergence of the velocity field. If the fluid is flowing inward (\( heta < 0\), convergence), the density increases. The negative sign ensures that inward flow increases \(\delta\).

  • \(3\dot{\phi}\): The gravitational redshift term. As the gravitational potential \(\phi\) decays or grows, it stretches or compresses the spacetime volume containing the fluid. This is a purely relativistic effect absent in Newtonian gravity, arising from the curvature of spacetime in the Newtonian gauge.

In the synchronous gauge (an alternative choice), the \(3\dot{\phi}\) term would appear differently or be absorbed into coordinate artifacts. The Newtonian gauge absorbs these effects into the potential, making the physics more transparent: matter falls into potential wells (\(\phi < 0\)), and as these wells deepen or shallow, the continuity equation adjusts accordingly.

Connection to the Euler Equation

The continuity equation is one of two fluid equations. The second is the Euler equation (momentum conservation), obtained from the spatial components \( abla_\mu T^{\mu i} = 0\):

\[\dot{ heta} + H heta = - rac{k^2}{a^2}\phi ag{46}\]

where \(k\) is the comoving wavenumber of the Fourier mode. This states that fluid acceleration is driven by the gradient of the gravitational potential, which is the general relativistic version of \(\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}\).

Together, these equations couple to Einstein’s equations to form a closed system. For CDM, this system predicts that density perturbations grow logarithmically with the scale factor during radiation domination, then linearly (\(\delta \propto a\)) during matter domination, which is the hallmark of gravitational instability that built the cosmic web.

Summary

We began with the Cosmological Principle and the Newtonian gauge, chose coordinates that make physics look like Newtonian gravity plus relativistic corrections, and derived from first principles how CDM density evolves. Starting from the definition of 4-velocity as the tangent to worldlines, we computed the perturbed components using the normalization condition \(u_\mu u^\mu = -1\), constructed the energy-momentum tensor, and applied the conservation law \( abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0\).

Our final result is the continuity equation for CDM:

\[ oxed{\dot{\delta} + heta - 3\dot{\phi} = 0} ag{47}\]

This equation is the first moment where gravity, motion, and spacetime stop being separate ideas and become a single dynamical system. From here on, structure is inevitable.

Stay tuned. The perturbations are about to become structure.

References:

[1] Ma, C.-P. & Bertschinger, E. (1995). “Cosmological Perturbation Theory in the Synchronous and Conformal Newtonian Gauges,” The Astrophysical Journal, 455, 7.

[2] Dodelson, S. & Schmidt, F. (2021). Modern Cosmology (2nd Ed.), Academic Press.

[3] Weinberg, S. (2008). Cosmology, Oxford University Press.

[4] Kodama, H. & Sasaki, M. (1984). “Cosmological Perturbation Theory,” Progress of Theoretical Physics Supplement, 78, 1-166.

[5] Malik, K. A. & Wands, D. (2009). “Cosmological Perturbations,” Physics Reports, 475, 1-51.

[6] Baumann, D. (2018). “Cosmology: Part III Mathematical Methods,” Cambridge lecture notes, arXiv:0907.5424.

[7] Bardeen, J. M. (1980). “Gauge-Invariant Cosmological Perturbations,” Physical Review D, 22, 1882-1905.

[8] Lifshitz, E. M. (1946). “On the Gravitational Stability of the Expanding Universe,” Zhurnal Eksperimentalnoi i Teoreticheskoi Fiziki, 16, 587.
